introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography (0750), Paper 3, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2025. Duration: three and a quarter hours.**

Answer ALL THE THREE QUESTIONS.

Question ONE carries THIRTY-FOUR marks and the rest carry THIRTY-THREE marks each.

In answering questions on this paper, you are encouraged to refer to your own field and practical work where relevant. Credit will be awarded for such references.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Non Programmable Calculators Are Allowed.

Materials required: Topographic map, Graph Paper and Photograph.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION C: FIELDWORK AND PROJECT-BASED LEARNING**

3. EITHER

Based on fieldwork you have carried out either in Physical or Human Geography, choose ONE of the Following topics:

(i) Weather characteristics

(ii) Coastal processes

(iii) Soil characteristics

(iv) Traffic flow characteristics

(v) Rural or Urban land use/characteristics

(vi) Agricultural or Industrial systems
incertitudes: Structure et règle de choix : la page de garde impose « Answer ALL THE THREE QUESTIONS » (question 1 = 34 points, questions 2 et 3 = 33 points) ; les questions 1 (SECTION A) et 2 (SECTION B) sont donc obligatoires et n'ont pas de règle. La question 3 (SECTION C) offre « EITHER ... OR » : codée en deux fichiers, « 3 » (EITHER, travail de terrain) et « 3-OR » (OR, projet), avec `regles_choix` « 1 parmi 2 » en SECTION C, identique dans les quatre fichiers. Cette consigne (3 questions, toutes obligatoires) diffère de celles des autres années (4 questions dont 1 ou 2 à choisir par section).

Carte de Santa : contrairement aux autres années, la carte topographique, sa légende, la photographie (question 1(d)) et le fond de carte du Cameroun (question 2(c)(i)) figurent dans le PDF (pages 5 à 7) et sont recadrés en PNG. C'est une reproduction réduite et de qualité moyenne : toutes les lectures du corrigé (altitudes, longueurs, noms de ruisseaux, forme de la ville) sont des lectures de cette reproduction, mesurées avec le carroyage de 1 km, donc approximatives (altitudes à quelques dizaines de mètres, longueurs à environ 0,3 km) ; les noms de ruisseaux sont illisibles. Elles sont à confronter à la carte originale (1:50 000) fournie le jour de l'examen. Le croquis du corrigé (fig-5 de la question 1) est schématique, compilé à partir de la carte.

Question 1(c)(i) : l'indice de détour est mesuré sur la reproduction : route environ 8,0 km (suivie le long du tracé, y compris le lacet près de la « Mile 8 junction »), distance en ligne droite environ 6,3 km, soit un indice d'environ 1,27 (127 pour cent). Le résultat dépend du point de départ choisi pour « Mile 12 (1751) » (carré de grille 17-51) et du point d'arrivée sur le cadre nord de la carte ; le corrigé accepte une valeur entre 1,2 et 1,35 et insiste sur la méthode.

Question 1(a)(i) : la légende imprime « Main Contour (100 m) », « Minor Contour (20 m) » et « Contour interval = 10 m » : indications incohérentes recopiées telles quelles (le corrigé ne s'appuie que sur les altitudes lues). Question 1(a)(iv) et (b) : « Bafut Ngemba Forest » est lue comme une réserve forestière protégée (la carte porte un tracé en tirets à sa limite sud) ; la situation générale de Santa (route vers Akum et Bamenda au nord, vers l'ouest des Hautes Terres au sud) dépasse la feuille : formulée avec prudence. Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées, sans statistique précise non certaine ; à relire par un géographe avant mise en avant. Le barème détaillé des corrigés est une proposition de répartition des points imprimés.

Question 1(d)(i) : la photographie (page 6) n'est accompagnée d'aucun lieu ni date ; elle montre un habitat spontané dense (tôles, planches, pneus sur les toits, pas de voirie visible) devant un quartier planifié. Le corrigé l'identifie comme un bidonville (habitat informel) et note que l'énoncé n'en donne pas la localisation.

Question 2(a) : « Source: Hypothetical » (données fictives) ; le tableau imprime tantôt « Bonduma » (ligne 8, voisin), tantôt « Bondouma » (ligne 9, village) : recopié tel quel. n = 11 villages, A = 50 km2 : d moyen = 20,5 / 11 = 1,8636 km ; Rn = 2 x 1,8636 x racine(11/50) = 1,748, soit 1,75 (1,74 si l'on utilise la moyenne arrondie à 1,86). Calculs vérifiés avec Python.

Question 2(b)(i) : le tableau imprime déjà 19, 6, 31 et 44 pour cent et 112 degrés pour le travail ; 112 correspond à 31 pour cent x 3,6 (arrondi), donc les degrés manquants sont calculés avec les pourcentages arrondis (68, 22, 158 ; total 360). Avec les fréquences brutes on obtiendrait 67,5 / 22,5 / 112,5 / 157,5 (total 360), valeurs acceptables. Le diagramme circulaire du corrigé (fig-2) est dessiné avec un rayon de 4 cm.

Question 2(c) : le titre du tableau 3 et l'énoncé imprimé disent « 2012 estimate » alors que la colonne porte « Population (2023 est.) » : écart d'impression recopié tel quel. « Let 3cm be the maximum circle size » est ambigu (diamètre ou rayon) : le corrigé retient 3 cm de diamètre pour le plus grand cercle (un rayon de 3 cm déborderait sur les petits cercles de la carte) et donne aussi les valeurs pour un rayon de 3 cm. Sur le fond de carte, le point à côté de « Buea » est retenu pour Buea (le point voisin, au nord-est, correspond à Kumba, dont le nom est imprimé au-dessus). Le fond de carte porte « Towns » en légende, non remplie. fig-3 est un modèle de réponse dessiné sur le fond de carte réduit.

Question 3 (SECTION C) : les réponses dépendent du travail de terrain ou du projet personnel du candidat ; le corrigé est une méthode et un exemple illustratif (comptages de trafic ; gestion des déchets d'un quartier) sans aucune donnée chiffrée inventée : toute réponse cohérente, précise et localisée est acceptée. questions.enonce_markdown: (a) Using a sketch map, locate the area of your fieldwork investigation. (5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
*The answer depends on the fieldwork of the candidate. Below, a model answer is built on one illustrative investigation, topic (iv) traffic flow characteristics along the main road of a town of the candidate's region (for example, Bamenda, Bafoussam or Buea); no results are invented and each candidate uses his or her own place, dates and findings. The same plan fits the other topics.*

**(a) Location sketch map (5 marks).** Draw a neat frame with a **title** (for example "Location of the traffic count sites along the main road of [town]"), a **north arrow**, a **scale** (a scale line or a ratio) and a **key** (1 mark each). Then place the study area in its setting, working from the general to the particular (2 marks for the location and 1 mark for neatness): the country or Region and the nearest big town, then the main road and neighbourhoods studied, with the **sampling sites** (for example counting stations A to D from the town centre to the outskirts) marked with symbols and labelled, and the main features that matter to the study (junctions, market, school, roundabout, river). Add a short note giving the distance from your school or from the nearest town.

*Marks: title 1, north and scale 1, key 1, correct location and sites 1.5, neatness and labels 0.5.*

questions.enonce_markdown: (b) State your objective and hypothesis that guided your investigation of the topic. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(b) Objective and hypothesis (3 marks).** The **objective** (aim) states what the study wants to find out; the **hypothesis** is a testable statement that the data will confirm or reject (1 mark for each plus 1 mark for a correct link between them).

*Illustration (traffic flow):* **Objective** - to find out how the volume and the type of traffic change along the main road from the town centre to the outskirts and with the time of the day. **Hypothesis** - "Traffic flow is heavier at the town centre than on the outskirts, and heavier at peak hours (morning and evening) than at other times."

*Other topics:* (i) weather: temperature and humidity are lower under tree cover than in an open space; (ii) coastal processes: the beach is steeper where the waves are stronger; (iii) soil: soil depth and humus content decrease with the slope angle; (v) land use: the intensity of land use decreases with distance from the town centre; (vi) agriculture or industry: the size of farms or factories is related to the distance from the market.

questions.enonce_markdown: (c) Outline the main type of data needed to verify the hypothesis. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(c) Types of data (4 marks).** Name the types of data and say why each is needed (1 mark each, any four).

- **Primary data** collected in the field by the group: **traffic counts** by type of vehicle (motorcycles, taxis, buses, private cars, trucks) and direction at each site during fixed periods (quantitative data).
- **Time and location data:** the time of day, the day of the week and the position of each counting site (distance from the centre), needed to compare sites and periods.
- **Qualitative data:** observations of road width and surface, junctions, parked vehicles and congestion, and short interviews with drivers, traders or traffic officers on the reasons for the flow (qualitative data).
- **Secondary data:** town maps, traffic or road-safety reports from the council or transport office, and earlier studies, used to check and complete the field data.

questions.enonce_markdown: (d) Describe how your data was collected. (6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(d) Data collection (6 marks).** Describe the methods in the order in which they were carried out, with the instruments and the way errors were limited (1 mark for each developed point, 6 points).

- **Preparation:** the class or group was divided into teams, each with a counting station, a map, a stopwatch, a clipboard and a **tally sheet** (a recording form prepared beforehand and tested in a trial count).
- **Sampling:** counting stations were chosen **systematically** along the road (at equal intervals from the centre to the outskirts), and counts were made on the same day of the week at **peak and off-peak hours** (for example 7-8 am, 12-1 pm and 5-6 pm).
- **Counting:** at each station, vehicles passing in each direction were tallied by type for **15 minutes (or 10 minutes) every hour**; each team had two members, one to count and one to record.
- **Observation and interviews:** a short field sheet was used to note road width, surface and junction type, and a questionnaire was given to a **random sample** of drivers and traders about the origin and the purpose of the journey.
- **Control of errors:** the counts were repeated on another day, all teams started and stopped at the same time, and the sheets were checked by the teacher before leaving the site.
- **Secondary data** were collected from the council to complete the primary data.

questions.enonce_markdown: (e) How was your data analyzed and presented? (6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(e) Analysis and presentation (6 marks).** Say what was done to the data and why each technique suits it (1 mark for each developed point).

- **Tables:** the tally sheets were totalled (counts per station, per vehicle type, per hour) and put in summary tables.
- **Descriptive statistics:** the **mean**, the **range** and **percentages** per vehicle type were calculated to compare the sites and the times.
- **Graphs:** **line graphs** of the hourly flow to show the peaks, **bar graphs or divided bars** for the vehicle types, and **pie charts** for the share of each type.
- **Maps:** **flow lines** (lines whose width is proportional to the number of vehicles) or **located bar graphs** drawn on a **sketch map** of the road to show the spatial pattern.
- **Statistical test (if the data allow):** the **Spearman rank correlation** between the distance from the centre and the traffic volume, to test the hypothesis, with the significance interpreted from the tables.
- **Interpretation and presentation:** the results were described, compared with the hypothesis and written up in a report with photographs, a title, a key and the source of each figure.

questions.enonce_markdown: (f) What were your findings in relation to the hypothesis and conclusion? (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown: **(f) Findings and conclusion (4 marks).** Each candidate gives the real results of his or her own study (1 mark for each point): the main pattern found (for example, the highest counts were recorded at the stations nearest the centre and at the peak hours, and the lowest on the outskirts), the **evidence** from the figures, the statement whether the hypothesis was **accepted, partly accepted or rejected**, and a short **conclusion** with the reasons for the pattern (market, offices and junctions near the centre, concentration of taxis and motorcycles, narrow roads). Do not give invented numbers: quote the results actually obtained, or give them in general terms (for example "about twice as many vehicles in the centre as on the outskirts") only if they are your own.

questions.enonce_markdown: (g) State one problem encountered during the investigation and how it was overcome. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown: **(g) Problem and solution (3 marks).** Name a **real problem** (1 mark), say how it affected the work (1 mark) and how it was **overcome** (1 mark). Examples: *rain or very hot weather* interrupted the counts (the counts were repeated on another day under comparable conditions); *heavy traffic and noise* made counting difficult and caused errors (each station had two counters, the tally sheets were simple and the counts were done in short periods); *refusal of some drivers to answer* (the aim of the study was explained and the sample was enlarged); *lack of time or of equipment* (the work was shared among teams and a trial was done beforehand); *road safety* (the counters stood on the pavement with an adult).

questions.enonce_markdown: (h) Of what significance was the fieldwork to your community? (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown: **(h) Significance for the community (2 marks, 1 each).** The results can **help the council and the transport and road-safety services** to plan traffic management (one-way streets, parking, signs, speed limits, an extra bus line or a bypass) and reduce congestion and accidents; the study also **raised awareness** among drivers and residents about road safety and pollution, gave local data for planning, and trained the students in field methods useful for later studies or work.
